Comparison with other software

Source: vignettes/articles/software-comparison.Rmd
software-comparison.Rmd

GCMSprime is the only workflow in this comparison that combines an estimated time-varying point-spread function (PSF) with compound-specific peak shapes, grouped peak selection across mass channels and a noise-aware information criterion for the final compound set.

The time-varying PSF supplies candidate peaks. Grouped feature selection uses the evidence across all ions to call each candidate, and refinement gives each compound its own log-concave elution profile. The final model fits a smooth background jointly with the peaks and uses the chosen noise family in the rank criterion. For overdispersed detector counts, the default is quasi-Poisson and the criterion is quasi-GIC. Mathematical basis

Benchmark on 16 simulated chromatograms

The simulation contains 48 compounds with retention-time drift, concentration-dependent peak shapes and partial presence across samples. Each chromatogram has 1,200 scans and 258 mass channels. GCMSprime estimated the PSF from the chromatograms and used quasi-Poisson with the simulation’s dispersion of 2. It recovered all 380 true peak occurrences with zero false calls.

The area plots show positive one-to-one matches within ±7.2 seconds and with a nominal-mass cosine of at least 0.70. Estimated areas use the units reported by the engine. Each panel shows adjusted R² and a 95% prediction interval for the log–log regression. The dashed 1:1 line applies to integrated counts.

For each true occurrence, the violin plot shows its best spectral hit anywhere in the sample and its best hit within ±7.2 seconds. A recovered spectrum can be the best hit for several occurrences. The counts indicate how many of the 380 occurrences had a candidate.

GCMSbenchmark includes the simulation recipe, engine settings, scoring tables and code to recreate both figures. The multisample tutorial gives the GCMSprime call, timing and disk-backed workflow.

Workflow differences

Workflow How it deconvolves and where that can limit recovery Access
GCMSprime Fits scan-level profiles and full spectra, with a compound-count penalty. A batch can share spectra while each sample retains its own profiles. Free, GPL open source. Repository
MS-DIAL Extracts spectra from detected model peaks within each run, then aligns the features. Smoothing, detection thresholds and the deconvolution window affect which components are recovered. GC–MS tutorial Free, LGPL-3 source. Some vendor readers have separate terms. MsdialWorkbench
mzmine / ADAP-GC The benchmark’s GC-EI module groups resolved ions by retention time and shape similarity. Pseudospectra depend on upstream detection, the grouping thresholds and the minimum number of ions. Batch alignment follows extraction. GC-EI guide Free Community licence for eligible academic users. Commercial use requires a paid plan. Public source · Plans
xcms + CAMERA Detects ion peaks first and then groups them into pseudospectra. Filter widths and grouping rules affect the coverage of weak and coeluting peaks. CAMERA was developed for LC–MS feature annotation. Kuhl et al. (2012) Free, GPL open source. xcms · CAMERA
eRah Uses local covariance and orthogonal signal deconvolution after filtering and baseline removal. Recovery depends on width and signal thresholds. Cross-sample alignment follows per-sample deconvolution. eRah manual Free, GPL open source. CRAN
AMDIS Uses representative ion traces as model peak shapes within each chromatogram. Component width, sensitivity and shape settings govern the calls and extracted spectra. NIST guide Free standalone binary. NIST distribution
GNPS/MSHub Requires a sample series for its NMF workflow. It factorizes aligned peak integrals, so the model resolves spectra and abundances from variation across samples and drops the scan-level profile information. Aksenov et al. (2021) · Workflow guide Free hosted workflow with a GNPS account. Public source under the repository’s nonprofit-use licence. Source · Licence
PARADISe Fits PARAFAC2 within retention intervals. Intervals and ranks can require review, and the constant cross-product constraint restricts how peak overlap can change across samples. Johnsen et al. (2017) · Protocol Free Community and paid Professional editions. Kromath
